hook: Did you know a court found out what a luxury bag costs to put together?

beats.say: In June 2024, a court in Milan put a company that makes Dior bags under its watch for one year.
The court papers said a small workshop got 53 euros to put one bag together. In the shop, the bag cost 2,600 euros.
In a case about Armani, one bag cost 93 euros, then 250, then 1,800 euros in the shop.
The workshops were in Italy, not in China. And the brands were not charged.

gfx.l: the workshops were in Italy, not China

takeaway: So the shop price and the making price can be very far apart.
confidence: high - 53/2,600 (Reuters, citing the court document) and 93/250/1,800 (WWD/Sourcing Journal, court findings) confirmed. 53 euros is the subcontractor's charge to supply the bag, not the full product cost. Court administration of the Armani unit was later lifted; neither brand was criminally investigated.
label: A court revealed what a *luxury bag* costs to *assemble*

hook: Did you know more than half of the world's shoes come from one country?

beats.say: In 2024, the world made almost 24 billion pairs of shoes.
About 13 billion of them came from China. That is more than half.
Almost nine out of ten pairs were made in Asia.
India is number two. Vietnam is number three.

takeaway: That is why so many shoes start on the China side.
confidence: high - World Footwear Yearbook 2025 (APICCAPS) figures for 2024; these are industry estimates.
label: *Half* of all shoes on Earth come from *one country*

hook: Did you know "Made in Italy" does not mean all of it was made in Italy?

beats.say: In the EU, a product gets one home country, even if many countries helped make it.
The label shows where the last big step happened. Not where every part came from.

gfx.l: the label follows the last step

beats.say: In 2017, The Guardian wrote that some Louis Vuitton shoes were mostly made in Romania, then finished in Italy.
That was reported as legal under the EU rule.

takeaway: The label shows the last step, not the whole trip.
confidence: high - Art. 60(2) Union Customs Code wording confirmed on the EC site; the Louis Vuitton example is attributed to The Guardian (June 2017), read via secondary summaries. It concerns Romania, not China.
label: *Made in Italy* doesn't mean what you think

hook: Did you know China sends more than 170 billion parcels in one year?

beats.say: In 2024, China counted 174.5 billion parcels.
That is 21 percent more than the year before.
It is about 478 million parcels every single day.
China has been number one in the world for 11 years in a row.

takeaway: That is one reason sending a parcel inside China is so cheap.
confidence: high - official State Post Bureau figures. 'Scale makes it cheap' and 'within days' are reasonable inferences, not sourced statistics.
label: China ships *170 billion* parcels a year

hook: Did you know there is a market in China with about 75,000 shops inside?

beats.say: It is in a city called Yiwu, in China.
It is bigger than 5 million square metres.
One minute at each shop, eight hours a day, would take about five months.
It started in 1982 as a small street market.

gfx.l: started as a small street market

takeaway: A lot of small things you see online pass through places like this.
confidence: medium - 75,000 booths is consistent across sources; floor area is quoted as 5.5 million or 6.4 million square metres, hence 'more than 5 million'. The five-month figure is arithmetic (75,000 minutes / 480 per day = 156 days).
label: A market with *75,000* booths

hook: Did you know two shopping apps filled about 88 big cargo planes a day?

beats.say: In early 2024, Reuters shared numbers about Shein and Temu.
Shein sent about 5,000 tonnes by air every day. Temu sent about 4,000.
Together, that is about 88 big cargo planes, full, every day.
In 2023, a US report said the two apps sent more than 30 percent of America's small duty-free parcels.

gfx.l: of US duty-free small parcels (2023 estimate)

takeaway: A lot of the China side now flies straight to shoppers.
confidence: medium - consultancy and committee estimates from 2023-2024, clearly dated in the script; volumes will have shifted after the 2025-2026 duty changes.
label: Two apps filled *88 cargo planes* a day

hook: Ever wondered what a shopping agent does?

beats.say: Taobao, Weidian and 1688 are shopping sites made for people in China.
A shopping agent buys the item for you and gets it sent to their warehouse.

gfx.l: the agent buys it for you

beats.say: There, they open it and take photos. These are called QC photos.

gfx.l: quality check photos of your item

beats.say: You see your real item before it leaves China. Then they ship it to you.

gfx.l: you see it before it leaves China

takeaway: That is how people buy from the China side.
confidence: medium - process description is consistent across agents, but the sources are agents' own guides (commercial, not independent). No numbers claimed.
label: What a *shopping agent* actually does

hook: Did you know most Nike sneakers today are not made in China?

beats.say: Nike publishes this in its annual report. In fiscal 2025, Vietnam made about 51 percent of Nike brand footwear.
Indonesia made about 28 percent. China made about 17 percent.
Those shoes came from 97 contract factories in 11 countries. Nike doesn't own them.
Adidas reports something similar. 92 percent of its volume comes from Asia, with Vietnam the biggest at 27 percent.

takeaway: So the big-brand map is Vietnam first, and China's factories increasingly serve other customers.
confidence: high - Nike figures quoted from its FY2025 Form 10-K. Adidas 27 percent / 92 percent are total volume (all product types), not footwear only.

hook: Did you know one of the biggest sneaker makers publishes its average price per pair?

beats.say: Yue Yuen is a giant contract shoemaker listed in Hong Kong. It makes shoes for major sports brands.
In 2024 it shipped about 255 million pairs.
Its average selling price to brands was about 20 dollars a pair.
That's an average across all its shoes, not the cost of any one model.
The rest of the shop price covers design, marketing, shipping, taxes, stores and profit.

takeaway: Factory price and shelf price are very different numbers, and China-side prices sit closer to the first.
confidence: high - 255.3 million pairs and US$20.25 average selling price are from Yue Yuen's FY2024 results. Brand customers are kept generic.

hook: Did you know couriers can charge you for the air inside a shoe box?

beats.say: It's called volumetric weight. Planes run out of space before they run out of lifting power.
DHL Express multiplies length, width and height in centimetres, then divides by 5,000.
You pay for whichever is bigger. The real weight or the volumetric weight.
A box of 33 by 22 by 12 centimetres counts as about 1.7 kilos, even if it's lighter.
That's why bulky, light things like boxed shoes and puffer jackets cost more to fly.

takeaway: So when you look at China-side prices, remember shipping depends on size as well as weight.
confidence: high - DHL's own formula; the shoe-box example is arithmetic (33 x 22 x 12 = 8,712; / 5,000 = 1.74 kg) with illustrative box dimensions. Other carriers use different divisors.

hook: Did you know the US used to let 4 million small parcels in duty-free every day?

beats.say: The rule was called de minimis. Packages worth 800 dollars or less came in without import duty.
US Customs says it processed 1.36 billion of these shipments in fiscal year 2024.
On May 2, 2025, the exemption ended for goods from China and Hong Kong.
On August 29, 2025, it was suspended for every country.
So now low-value imports into the US face duties and paperwork. Rules keep changing, so check official sources.

takeaway: If you're looking at the China side from the US, the landed cost is a different sum now.
confidence: high - CBP primary sources for both dates and the 1.36 billion figure. Rules are still moving (a June 2026 Federal Register notice covers postal shipments); re-check before publishing.

hook: Did you know the EU now charges a flat 3 euro duty on small parcels?

beats.say: For years, parcels worth under 150 euros entered the European Union with no customs duty.
In December 2025, EU governments agreed to end that.
Since July 1, 2026, there's a fixed duty of 3 euros.
And it's per type of item, not per parcel. Three different products can mean three charges.
The EU calls it temporary, until a full new customs system is ready, expected around 2028.

takeaway: So if you compare China-side prices from Europe, add that duty to your maths.
confidence: high - Council of the EU press release (12 Dec 2025) and Commission notice (29 June 2026). The duty applies per tariff heading in a consignment; import VAT is separate and not covered.

hook: Did you know China's share of world clothing exports is actually shrinking?

beats.say: According to World Trade Organization data, China had 29.6 percent of world clothing exports in 2024.
That's still huge. But it's the lowest share since 2010.
Here's the twist. China's share of textile exports, meaning fabric and yarn, went up to 43.3 percent.
So a shirt sewn in Vietnam or Bangladesh is often made from Chinese fabric.

takeaway: Even when the label says another country, part of the story often starts in China.
confidence: high - WTO figures as compiled by Prof. Sheng Lu (University of Delaware). 'Often made from Chinese fabric' is a general pattern, not a rule for every garment.

hook: Ever wondered why posting a small packet from China used to cost almost nothing?

beats.say: Postal services pay each other to deliver foreign mail. The fees are called terminal dues.
They're set by the Universal Postal Union, a body founded back in 1874.
For years those fees were low for small packets from many countries, including China.
In 2018 the United States threatened to leave the union over it.
So in September 2019, members agreed a reform. Big importers could start setting their own rates from July 2020.

takeaway: Postage rules shape prices, which is why China-side shipping costs have changed since then.
confidence: high - UPU and USPS primary sources for the 25 September 2019 decision and the July 2020 self-declared rates. Contested subsidy-size estimates are left out.

hook: Did you know the world's biggest shopping event started with just 27 shops?

beats.say: November 11, written 11.11, began as an informal "singles' day" among Chinese students.
In 2009 Alibaba ran a sale that day with only 27 merchants. Sales were about 50 million yuan.
By 2021 Alibaba alone reported 540 billion yuan over its 11-day event. About 84 billion dollars.
For 2025, data firm Syntun estimated nearly 1.7 trillion yuan across all platforms.
Those are gross sales estimates over several weeks now, not one single day.

takeaway: It's a good reminder of how big the China-side shopping world really is.
confidence: high for 2009 and 2021 (Alibaba-reported, via Reuters/CNBC); medium for 2025 (third-party Syntun estimate).

hook: Taobao, 1688, Weidian. Do you know what actually makes them different?

beats.say: 1688 is Alibaba's wholesale site for buyers inside China. It dates back to 1999.
Taobao came in 2003. It's mostly small shops selling to regular shoppers.
Weidian launched in 2014. It let anyone open a tiny shop from a phone and share it on social apps.
That same year a funding round led by Tencent put 350 million dollars into Weidian's parent company.

takeaway: Three platforms, three roles, and together they show most of what's on the China side.
confidence: medium - 1999 launch (Alibaba Group), Weidian's January 2014 launch and the 350 million dollar Tencent-led round are sourced; the Weidian facts rely on trade press rather than company filings.

hook: Did you know Taobao was started in an apartment to take on eBay?

beats.say: In 2003 eBay invested in EachNet, then China's biggest online auction site.
That same year, on May 10, a small Alibaba team launched Taobao from an apartment in Hangzhou.
The goal was to compete with eBay EachNet for person-to-person selling in China.
Alibaba already ran a wholesale marketplace, launched in 1999. Taobao was its move into everyday shopping.

takeaway: Today it's an everyday shopping app in China, and a window into what's sold there.
confidence: medium - launch date, apartment origin and the eBay EachNet rivalry are documented, but the main source for the detail is Baidu Baike (encyclopaedia, not primary).

hook: Ever wondered why one Chinese city, Putian, is so tied to sneakers?

beats.say: Putian is a city in Fujian province, on China's south-east coast.
From the 1980s, factories there made shoes on contract for big foreign sports brands.
That built a whole local network of sole makers, material suppliers and skilled workers.
In 2010 the New York Times reported that copy makers there simply bought real pairs and reverse-engineered them.
So the popular story that copies are leftover originals from the brand's factory is mostly a myth.

takeaway: Knowing the real history helps you read what sellers on the China side actually claim.
confidence: medium - NYT Magazine (Nicholas Schmidle, 19 Aug 2010) is the anchor; the 1980s contract-manufacturing history also rests on lower-authority Chinese encyclopaedia sources. Unauthorised extra production does exist in some industries, hence 'mostly a myth'.
